asOf: 2026-09-19 rev2 (after red team R1-06, R1-07, R1-20)

reasons.peakYear: Every evening block in the evidence ran on a fixed night in 1996: ABC Friday, Nickelodeon Saturday, Nick at Nite nightly (sections 2.1, 2.2, 2.9). Fox Kids and Kids' WB ran fixed Saturday morning slots, which supports fixed slot, not fixed night.
reasons.memorySalience: Named as a defining feature by the retrospective press in the evidence (Looper, Deadline 2025, TV Insider 2022, Collider) for both evening blocks. Band 70 to 89 with a high placement. The 1993 kids 6 to 11 Saturday rating (section 2.2 item 5) is Wikipedia-only and unverified, so it does not lift the band to 90 plus.
reasons.reproducibility: A weekly premiere on a fixed night needs no partner and no spectrum. Mechanics table row 1.
reasons.expressionRisk: Pure structure. A day of the week cannot be owned.

reasons.peakYear: ABC and Nickelodeon both held 8 to 10 p.m. across 1996 (sections 2.1 and 2.2).
reasons.memorySalience: Named often. The 8 p.m. start is part of the recall for both blocks (section 2.2 item 1, section 2.1).
reasons.reproducibility: A live premiere can fix a time. On-demand play dilutes the lead-in effect that made the time matter (mechanics table row 2, Webster 2006).
reasons.ownerEffort: A scheduled publish. Light weekly work.

reasons.peakYear: Both ABC and Nickelodeon ran four half-hours in 1996 (sections 2.1 and 2.2).
reasons.memorySalience: Named for two blocks. Two shows fell after leaving the four-slot block in 1997 (section 2.1 items 15 to 18). Counter-evidence: one show posted its best season after leaving the block for a Tuesday slot (section 2.1 item 9). Band 70 to 89, low placement.
reasons.reproducibility: A four-episode playlist is native to streaming. Adams (1997) shows block tactics raise renewal, not rating, so the value is retention (section 2.10).
reasons.ownerEffort: Four pieces of content per week. Light scheduling work once the content exists.

reasons.peakYear: Disney launched a hosted Saturday block in 1997 while ABC cast members still hosted Friday (sections 2.1 item 5, 2.7 item 1).
reasons.memorySalience: The hosted wrap defined the ABC brand in retrospectives (section 2.1 item 5). Mixed evidence: Disney cut hosts in 2000 for low ratings (section 2.7 item 3).
reasons.reproducibility: Creator-hosted intros are standard on video platforms. But made-for-kids rules disable the host's engagement tools: comments, live chat, memberships (landscape.md section 4 and section 8). Hosting works as a recorded wrap without those tools. Band 70 to 89, low placement.
reasons.expressionRisk: The host style is an expressive surface that must be designed fresh. In-character cast hosting is a known device.
reasons.ownerEffort: A weekly production task with talent.

reasons.peakYear: Nick at Nite's branded interstitial model coincided with a 60 percent prime-time rise from Q1 1994 to Q1 1995 (section 2.9 item 2).
reasons.memorySalience: Named for two blocks: Nickelodeon shorts and couch bumpers, ABC animation and skits (mechanics table row 5).
reasons.reproducibility: Shorts and bumpers are cheap to produce and stitch (mechanics table row 5).
reasons.expressionRisk: Bumpers carry a visual identity that must be original.
reasons.ownerEffort: Light weekly production once a template exists.

reasons.peakYear: The 1997 stunt sent one character through every show in the lineup (section 2.1 item 12).
reasons.memorySalience: Named for two blocks: ABC 1991, 1996, 1997 and NBC 1991 (mechanics table row 6). No ratings link found.
reasons.reproducibility: Needs multiple shows with shared talent. Possible only once the slate exists.
reasons.expressionRisk: Structure, but the crossover device is associated with specific characters. The studio must use its own.
reasons.ownerEffort: A coordinated multi-show production. Weekly effort is high in crossover weeks only.

reasons.peakYear: Nickelodeon's 8 to 10 p.m. premise for kids too old for bed at eight held through the mid-1990s (section 2.2 item 3).
reasons.memorySalience: One block's premise, cited by one secondary source (Wikipedia quoting the network president) and one retrospective phrase (Looper). Band 40 to 69.
reasons.reproducibility: Timing can signal an event. The evidence file's mechanics table (row 7) says devices remove the parental gate. That is the analyst's judgment, not a sourced finding. The ritual kit must rebuild the gate. Band 40 to 69.
reasons.ownerEffort: Set by the schedule. Runs itself.

reasons.peakYear: Nickelodeon's couch ran 1992 to 1999 and Disney's hosted studio set launched in 1997 (sections 2.2 item 6, 2.7 item 1).
reasons.memorySalience: The couch anchored bumpers for seven years and drove a 1999 giveaway (section 2.2 items 6 and 7).
reasons.reproducibility: A recurring virtual or physical set is simple (mechanics table row 8).
reasons.expressionRisk: The mechanic is known mainly through one block's specific prop. The binding constraints forbid couch props. The set must be a different object entirely.

reasons.peakYear: No in-window event verified. The cited contest (1999) and countdown (2001) fall outside 1993 to 1998. Peak year is not used in the score after decision D-008.
reasons.memorySalience: Rarely named. Present but not recalled (mechanics table row 9).
reasons.reproducibility: Live chat, polls, and votes are native to digital. But made-for-kids rules disable comments and live chat. Participation must route through the parent account.
reasons.ownerEffort: Light weekly moderation through parent accounts.

reasons.peakYear: Nick at Nite's Block Party Summer began in 1994 (section 2.9 item 3).
reasons.memorySalience: Named for two blocks: the 1994 summer stunt and ABC's 1996 theme park episodes (mechanics table row 10).
reasons.reproducibility: Themed weeks and marathons map to playlists and events (mechanics table row 10).
reasons.expressionRisk: Structure. The theme is new each time.
reasons.ownerEffort: A production push a few times a year. Averaged to light weekly work.

reasons.peakYear: The ABC jingle and the Nick at Nite radio-style format both ran through the mid-1990s (sections 2.1 item 6, 2.9 item 1).
reasons.memorySalience: One verified block jingle (section 2.1 item 6, Looper and Deadline 2025). Nick at Nite's radio-style format is a programming metaphor, not a sonic ident. One block puts this in the 40 to 69 band, high placement.
reasons.reproducibility: Audio idents are cheap and persist across clips (mechanics table row 11).
reasons.expressionRisk: Known mainly through one block's jingle and lyric. The new ident must share nothing with it.
